item.title: Leaseback Structures Now Back Nearly Half of US Data Center Construction
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
Hyperscalers are becoming tenants in their own data centers

The post Leaseback Structures Now Back Nearly Half of US Data Center Construction appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
A few seconds agoNov. 16, 2026 5:20 pm

Ownership of the AI buildout is quietly separating from the companies doing the building. Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust agreed last week to acquire a majority stake in a data center portfolio from Amazon in a deal valued around $5 billion, taking 75.1 percent of two joint ventures holding 13 newly built powered shells across campuses in Indiana and Mississippi. Amazon Web Services keeps 24.9 percent, worth about $600 million, and leases back the entire portfolio on an initial 12-year term extending to 32 years if fully exercised. The portfolio carries 647 megawatts and priced at a 7 percent initial capitalization rate. BXDC funded it with roughly $1.9 billion of proceeds from the public offering it completed earlier this year plus about $2.5 billion in new non-recourse mortgage debt.

Amazon’s reason for selling buildings it intends to keep using is visible in its own disclosures. The company raised 2026 cash capital expenditure guidance to roughly $220 billion in July, up from $200 billion, which Andy Jassy attributed largely to higher memory costs, and held that figure steady at third-quarter earnings. Trailing twelve-month free cash flow swung to an outflow of $42.4 billion by the end of the third quarter, against a $14.8 billion inflow a year earlier, as trailing capital expenditure reached roughly $211 billion versus $168.3 billion of operating cash flow. Cash capital expenditures in the quarter alone were $75.9 billion.

Jassy has been direct about the timing problem underneath those numbers, noting that data center capital goes out roughly two years before the servers inside produce revenue and that free cash flow headwinds continue until the sites are monetized. AWS carries a backlog around $496 billion and grew 39 percent in the quarter, so the constraint is not demand. It is the lag between writing the check and collecting the rent, and a sale-leaseback shortens that considerably by converting a finished building into cash while keeping the capacity.

Meta has run the same play at larger scale and pioneered the template. Its Hyperion campus in Richland Parish, Louisiana, sits inside a special purpose vehicle managed by Blue Owl Capital that raised roughly $27 billion in external debt, with Meta holding 20 percent as minority partner and tenant and providing residual value guarantees near $28 billion. Meta announced a similar venture with BlackRock in El Paso at roughly $14 billion for a one-gigawatt campus, again taking 20 percent alongside the land and about $2.3 billion of construction. A third Texas venture followed at comparable size, returning $1.04 billion in cash to Meta.

The aggregate obligation created by all of this is now large enough that ratings agencies have started tracking it separately. Moody’s calculated that the five largest US hyperscalers held $969 billion in undiscounted future data center lease commitments at the end of 2025, with $662 billion sitting off balance sheet because the leases had not yet commenced. Later tallies put the uncommenced figure above $1 trillion, with Microsoft carrying the largest disclosed pipeline. The Bank for International Settlements described the mechanics in its March Quarterly Review as substituting upfront capital expenditure for multi-year operating expenses financed through dedicated vehicles backed by private credit.

Sizing the leaseback share against total development requires some estimation, since nobody publishes a clean tally. The Census Bureau put private US data center construction at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of about $85 billion in August, up 73 percent year over year, against $49.7 billion for all of 2025. The announced joint venture and leaseback structures over roughly the past eighteen months, counting Hyperion, El Paso, the second Texas venture, and now the AWS portfolio, total somewhere near $60 billion. Measured against perhaps $125 billion of US data center construction put in place over the same window, that suggests close to half the capital behind the largest projects is now arriving through structures where the operator is a tenant rather than an owner. The figure is imprecise and heavily weighted toward Meta, but the direction is not ambiguous.

Development economics change when the end buyer is identified before the slab is poured. A hyperscaler building for its own account underwrites against internal cost of capital and holds whatever it builds. A hyperscaler building for contribution to a venture underwrites against what a Blackstone or a Blue Owl will pay, which means cap rates, lease terms, and residual value assumptions start shaping design decisions the way they already do in industrial and net lease. The 7 percent cap rate on the AWS portfolio is a real number that other developers can price against, and the 12-year initial term with a 32-year extension is a real duration that lenders can underwrite.

What remains unresolved is who holds the risk when a 12-year lease expires on a building designed for hardware that turns over every four or five years. Powered shells age better than the equipment inside them, which is most of the argument for this asset class, but the residual value guarantees Meta attached to its ventures suggest the capital partners wanted something more than that argument. We would expect more of these transactions in 2027 given how much construction is still in the pipeline and how thin free cash flow has become across the group, and we would watch the guarantee terms more closely than the headline prices.

item.title: Geothermal Drilling Gains Traction as Data Centers Hunt Grid Capacity
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Bedrock Energy raised $24 million to expand geothermal drilling for commercial buildings and data centers seeking grid capacity relief.

The post Geothermal Drilling Gains Traction as Data Centers Hunt Grid Capacity appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Bedrock Energy closed a $24 million funding round to expand its AI-directed geothermal drilling operation for commercial buildings. The startup uses directional drilling techniques adapted from oil and gas extraction to install geothermal heat pump systems up to 1,000 feet deep. Bedrock claims its rigs cut drilling time by up to 80% compared to conventional water-well-style equipment, reducing installation costs for systems that use the earth as a year-round heat source and sink. The company currently operates in Texas, Utah, Colorado, New York, and Alberta.

Clean Energy Ventures and Clearvision Ventures led the round, joined by GVP Climate, Susquehanna Sustainable Investments, Catalytic Capital for Climate and Health by Temasek Trust, and several other investors. Bedrock raised $12 million in its Series A last year and $8.5 million in a 2023 seed round. The new capital will fund rig purchases and expansion into New England, New Jersey, the upper Midwest, and additional Western states. The company has drilled nine sites to date and secured commitments from customers planning installations over the next two years.

Data center developers have emerged as a customer segment alongside office and commercial properties. Some operators want geothermal cooling for server racks, but others see the technology as a way to free up grid capacity by deploying it on adjacent parcels. CEO Joselyn Lai said one Michigan prospect estimated that freeing a few megawatts could accelerate data center operations by months or a full year. Geothermal heat pumps require minimal maintenance once installed, making them attractive for long-term infrastructure projects where upfront costs can be amortized over decades of service.

item.title: Phoenix Midtown Gets Corporate Anchor as U-Haul Fills Distressed Tower
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
U-Haul consolidates 2,000 employees in a Phoenix tower bought from foreclosure, stabilizing a distressed midtown asset as the office market recovers selectively.

The post Phoenix Midtown Gets Corporate Anchor as U-Haul Fills Distressed Tower appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
U-Haul has moved 2,000 employees into a 25-story office tower at 20 East Thomas Road in Phoenix, completing its acquisition and renovation of the former CenturyLink building. The company paid $23.7 million for the 548,938-square-foot property in December 2024, two years after the building entered foreclosure through lender Second Step Asset Management, a Bank of America affiliate. The building was 84% vacant at acquisition. Only one tenant remains: HDR Engineering, which occupies 20,000 square feet and is negotiating to double its footprint.

U-Haul expanded from roughly 300,000 square feet in its previous Central Avenue headquarters to 500,000 square feet in the new building. CEO Joe Shoen said the company needed room to grow after filling all 22 floors of its original two-tower complex, where it had operated since relocating from Portland in 1967. The company retained ownership of its former headquarters and surrounding parcels between Central Avenue and 3rd Street, including a conference center and fitness facility that opened in 2021. Shoen said the old towers may be repurposed for self-storage or nonprofit office space, though no final plans have been set.

U-Haul employs nearly 4,000 people in Arizona and maintains a market capitalization above $10.6 billion. The company reported $137 million in earnings for its second fiscal quarter of 2027, up from $106 million the prior year, driven by self-storage and its U-Box portable container service, which together account for 25% of revenue. Self-storage revenue has grown 71% since the second quarter of fiscal 2022.

Phoenix office vacancy stood at 22% in the third quarter of 2026, down from 24% the prior year, but midtown Phoenix posted a 26.7% vacancy rate that has trended higher even as the broader market recovered. Midtown asking rents average 15% below market, with Class A buildings in top submarkets commanding nearly double midtown rates. CoStar analysts said the submarket is positioned to attract tenants seeking quality towers at discounted pricing, a profile U-Haul’s occupancy validates.

item.title: Real Estate Market Transparency Determines Where Global Capital Goes
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
JLL’s 2026 Global Real Estate Transparency Index reveals how data, legal frameworks, and market openness shape global property investment.

The post Real Estate Market Transparency Determines Where Global Capital Goes appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Every country runs its real estate market differently. Ownership records sit in different places and in different formats. Transaction prices are public in some jurisdictions and private in others. Valuation standards, lease conventions, foreclosure procedures, and tax treatment all vary in ways that are obvious to local participants and genuinely difficult for anyone arriving from outside. An investor evaluating a building in a market they do not know well is often working with less information than a local buyer and has fewer ways to check what they have been told.

JLL has been measuring those differences since 1999 through its Global Real Estate Transparency Index, which released its fourteenth edition in September. The 2026 version scores 88 countries and territories along with 146 city markets across 260 individual measures, weighted into six categories covering performance measurement, market fundamentals, governance of listed vehicles, regulatory and legal conditions, transaction process, and sustainability. Markets are placed in five tiers running from Highly Transparent to Opaque. Richard Bloxam, Chief Executive Officer of Global Capital Markets at JLL, says the project grew out of what the firm could observe across its own network. “We have offices all over the world and have for almost a century so we have been able to see what is similar and what is different,” he said. “We wanted to understand why some countries get so much investment while others don’t.”

The answer the index keeps producing is that transparency and capital travel together, and the relationship has been getting stronger rather than weaker. Thirteen countries currently occupy the Highly Transparent tier, led by the United Kingdom, France, Australia, and the United States. Transaction volumes in those markets rose 64 percent over the past two years, growing 20 percentage points faster than the rest of the world. That group now accounts for 56 percent of global income-producing real estate and more than 80 percent of all direct investment, roughly $1.4 trillion over the period.

Bloxam frames the index as a guide to how much work a market will require rather than a list of places worth avoiding. “By benchmarking how transparent these markets are as a way to guide occupiers and investors as to where they would have an easier path,” he said. “We don’t think it means that you shouldn’t invest in less transparent markets, just that it will be a bit more work to do so effectively.” Capital does go into opaque markets, generally at wider spreads and with more local partnership involved.

What tends to get overlooked in discussions of data transparency is the legal infrastructure sitting behind it, which the index weights heavily. Regulatory and legal conditions carry 23.5 percent of the total score, second only to performance measurement. Bloxam points to enforcement as the question most foreign investors underestimate. “Legal framework is really important,” he said. “Can lenders enforce if a loan is breached? You take that for granted but it isn’t a given in every market.” A lender willing to finance a deal in a jurisdiction where remedies are slow or uncertain will price that uncertainty in, which raises the cost of capital for everyone operating there.

Listed vehicles do work that is harder to see. A REIT regime creates a population of companies filing public financials, disclosing portfolio details, and reporting performance on a schedule, which generates market information as a byproduct of regulatory compliance. The index assigns 10 percent of its scoring to governance of listed vehicles for that reason. “The formation of REITs is really important,” Bloxam said. “Many countries now have their own program of tax-efficient investment vehicles. Countries that do that well are able to get higher ratings.” The disclosure obligations attached to those vehicles give everyone in the market a reference point for pricing, including investors who will never buy a share.

Cross-border capital gets most of the attention in these conversations, though it is not the whole picture. Domestic investors operate with local knowledge, local relationships, and a tolerance for conditions that would deter an outsider, and that activity has proven durable through disruptions that stopped foreign capital cold. “There is a level of activity that seems to be pretty resilient,” Bloxam said. “Even during COVID there was market activity, suggesting that domestic investment carries on even in the face of all of the chaos.” Markets with deep domestic investor bases tend to keep transacting through periods when international capital withdraws.

The most pronounced improvements in the index have come from governments that decided transparency was worth pursuing deliberately. Saudi Arabia, Dubai, Abu Dhabi, and Qatar all rank among the most improved markets of the past decade despite regional disruption during that period. Saudi Arabia has built centralized databases for rents, sales prices, and transaction volumes as part of Vision 2030, along with enhanced standards for listed companies, while the Dubai Land Department has become a leader in publishing real-time, publicly accessible real estate data. “The Middle East has done a really great job of making transparency part of their broader policy agenda,” Bloxam said. “They really want to attract capital and make their countries more efficient.”

Two-thirds of the markets in this year’s index improved their scores, with Asia Pacific posting the strongest regional gains. India, Vietnam, South Korea, Australia, and Thailand accounted for half of the top ten global improvers, and transaction volumes in India and Vietnam reached all-time highs.

Improvement at that pace does not appear to be narrowing the distance at the top, which is the uncomfortable finding in this year’s index. The most transparent markets are pulling away faster than anyone is catching up, which means the largest and most liquid transactions will keep concentrating in a small set of countries even as conditions get better everywhere else. For governments trying to attract capital, the work that moves the needle tends to be unglamorous and slow, involving land registry digitization, disclosure requirements for listed companies, and enforceable creditor remedies. The markets climbing the index fastest are the ones that stopped treating those as administrative matters and started treating them as economic policy.

item.title: From Occupancy Data to Action: How CRE Leaders Should Plan for 2027
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Studio
item.description:
Occupancy data helps office owners prioritize upgrades, optimize staffing and amenities, benchmark performance, and reduce leasing risk.

The post From Occupancy Data to Action: How CRE Leaders Should Plan for 2027 appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Office owners are being asked to improve their buildings in a market that has made improvement expensive. Financing costs remain high, valuations have not fully recovered, and the flight to quality has left mid-tier assets competing against newer products with better amenities and fewer deferred capital needs. Tenants touring space now arrive with sharper expectations and more alternatives, which means the buildings that cannot keep up tend to lose deals before an owner understands why.

Most owners have a shorter list of things they can fund than things they would like to fix. A lobby renovation, an amenity floor, a chiller replacement, and a leasing concession budget all compete for the same dollars, and the decision usually gets made on instinct and broker feedback rather than on evidence about how the building is being used. Picking wrong is expensive in two directions, since the capital is gone and the problem that actually needed solving remains.

Occupancy data has become useful for exactly that prioritization, and a number of owners are discovering they have more of it than they realized. Access control systems have been recording entries for years, often without anyone treating the output as something to analyze.

Haniel Lynn, Chief Executive Officer of Kastle Systems, says the limitation can sometimes be how the data is organized rather than in what equipment exists. “Customers often want to know what they need to put in place,” he said. “In many cases, the systems are already there. The challenge is connecting the data in a way that provides meaningful insights into how spaces are being used.” 

As a managed physical security provider, Kastle helps commercial property owners and operators connect access control, video security, and other building technologies to turn everyday security data into actionable operational insights. A badge swipe recorded as an access event answers a security question. The same swipe connected to a tenant, a floor, and a pattern over time answers an operating question.

Whether an owner needs to invest in collecting more occupancy data depends on what they are trying to decide. “Every company should think hard about how much granularity they need when it comes to occupancy data,” he said. “Sometimes things like occupancy sensors can cost a lot so you have to weigh that against the benefit.” Knowing which days a building fills up is enough to set cleaning schedules and staff a lobby. Knowing which specific conference rooms sit empty requires a different and considerably more expensive layer of instrumentation.

Staffing is where entry data pays off fastest, since labor is a recurring cost that can be adjusted without a capital request. A building running at full occupancy on Tuesday and Wednesday has a different labor profile than one that fills evenly across the week. Matching janitorial, security, and food and beverage expenses to actual patterns rather than to a uniform schedule reduces cost without sacrificing occupancy experience.

In a competitive office market, amenities are becoming more important as a way to stand out. Usage patterns will help buildings make better amenity decisions. High peak gym usage could help justify the ROI of expanding the facilities. New amenities or programming ideas can be tested before they are fully incorporated into the building.

Occupancy and usage data have long been used to help understand the likelihood of a lease renewal. Now,  AI has added a new layer to that analysis. “With AI, you can bring in other layers of information on top of the data you are already collecting,” Lynn said. “For example, you can pair occupancy data with news and job listing information of tenants to get a better sense of whether or not the company is growing or shrinking.” A tenant with falling attendance and an active hiring page is adjusting its schedule. A tenant with falling attendance, layoff coverage, and no open roles is a renewal risk worth preparing for well before the conversation starts. Owners who spot that early can start working the space, adjust concession assumptions in their budget, or approach the tenant about a restructure while there is still time to do it on favorable terms.

Building data often doesn’t mean much without a reference point. A building at 48 percent occupancy is performing well or poorly depending entirely on what comparable buildings in the same market are running. “Benchmarking is a really important part of noticing patterns,” Lynn said. “You need to know how a building or organization is doing compared to others.” An owner evaluating whether to spend on a lobby renovation needs to know whether the building is underperforming its peer set or whether the whole submarket is soft, and those two situations call for different responses.

Since 2020, Kastle’s Back to Work Barometer has provided a consistent view of office occupancy trends, using anonymized access control data from thousands of buildings in ten major U.S. cities.  The series has gotten considerably more granular over time, and some of the most useful splits have come from separating building classes. An owner comparing a Class B asset against a national average that includes trophy product is measuring against the wrong benchmark.

Occupancy data gives owners something to check those assumptions against. A floor that has sat empty for two years raises a question about whether renovating it will attract a tenant or whether the capital belongs in shared amenity space serving the tenants already in the building. A mechanical system running on a schedule built for full occupancy may be a candidate for controls work rather than replacement.

Owners making these decisions over the next few years will be working with patterns that are still moving. Attendance has been climbing, the midweek concentration has held for three years running, and the distance between the best buildings and everything else has widened rather than narrowed. Leasing assumptions built on 2021 behavior are already out of date, and the owners checking their decisions against current data are the ones most likely to spend their limited capital on the things that change outcomes.

The post From Occupancy Data to Action: How CRE Leaders Should Plan for 2027 appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Data Centers Push Small Nuclear Reactors Toward First US Deployment
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Carbon County, Utah approves conditional permit for startup to build up to 120 small modular reactors paired with data centers on state trust land.

The post Data Centers Push Small Nuclear Reactors Toward First US Deployment appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Carbon County, Utah planners approved a conditional use permit Thursday for Valar Atomics to build between 40 and 120 small modular reactors on 640 acres of state trust land near Wellington. Planning Commissioner Lisa Simmons cast the only dissenting vote at the special meeting in Price. Valar cannot break ground on reactors until the Nuclear Regulatory Commission issues licenses, and power plants must remain at least half a mile from homes. The company also must hold at least three public town halls and post a cleanup bond.

Valar joined the Energy Department’s Reactor Pilot Program in August 2025 and flew a test reactor to Utah from California aboard a military C-17 in February. That reactor went critical in June, sustaining a nuclear chain reaction independently. The company leases 480 acres from the Utah Trust Lands Administration under a 52-year agreement that paid the state a $400,000 signing bonus and carries annual rent of $14,400 during a five-year development phase, rising to $300,000 by year eight. The land previously generated about $4,000 annually, with proceeds funding K-12 schools in Utah.

Valar calls the approved project the Raceway Energy Campus and has proposed a far larger development called Project Beehive on adjacent federal land managed by the Bureau of Land Management. That plan envisions roughly 456 small reactors and data centers across more than 9,000 acres, with combined output of about 9.6 gigawatts—more than double Utah’s average production of four gigawatts. Only three new nuclear plants have come online in the United States since 2000.

The permit includes a natural gas plant to power manufacturing, lab, and data center buildings until reactors are built, then serve as backup. Democratic state Senator Nate Blouin of Millcreek called the gas plant a “bait-and-switch” after it appeared for the first time in the permit application. Valar’s timeline targets first reactor startup on federal land in 2028, though the Bureau of Land Management told NPR in September it was still reviewing whether that application was complete. Nearly 200 residents attended Thursday’s meeting, and local petitions have asked the county commission for a temporary moratorium on large energy projects.

item.title: Year-Round Lagoon Resorts Enter Mixed-Use Development Playbook
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
St. Charles advances sale of 19.5 acres for Missouri's first indoor lagoon resort, adding year-round beach amenity to $350 million riverfront district.

The post Year-Round Lagoon Resorts Enter Mixed-Use Development Playbook appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
St. Charles, Missouri has given preliminary approval to sell 19.5 acres of city-owned riverfront land for $4.15 million to Lux Haven Group LLC, a local developer proposing an enclosed lagoon beach resort and condominium complex. Beach Club at Riverpointe would feature a three-quarter-acre indoor lagoon under a climate-controlled dome, 150 to 315 condos, and 35,000 to 50,000 square feet of commercial space in its first phase. The project would be the first year-round indoor lagoon resort in Missouri. Final approval could come as soon as November 17.

Later phases would add a 200-room hotel, additional residential development, golf amenities, and other resort features. Marketing materials describe white sand, warm water, cabanas, a swim-up bar, waterfall, spa, and public access through day passes and memberships. Developer Lux Haven, led by St. Charles real estate investor William Schmitt, plans to break ground in spring 2027, open the beach later that year, and deliver first residential units in 2028. Development costs were not disclosed.

Beach Club joins the city’s $350 million Riverpointe district, a 120-acre riverfront redevelopment zone near Interstate 70 that already includes Chicken N Pickle and has a dual-branded hotel and at least 200 apartments under development by Edward Rose Properties. The land sale is contingent on additional agreements and would include tax incentives such as Community Improvement District and Transportation Development District designations, plus a temporary Chapter 100 property tax abatement. The project represents a new amenity category for mixed-use developments seeking to differentiate residential offerings in second-tier markets.

item.title: AI In Property Management Has a Ground-Truth Problem
item.dc:creator: Mike Laurie
item.description:
AI in property management needs more than connected data: verified building information, clear provenance and visible uncertainty are essential for trust.

The post AI In Property Management Has a Ground-Truth Problem appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Artificial intelligence has a remarkable ability to consume building information. Give it drawings, specifications, inspection reports, maintenance records, leases, photographs and spreadsheets, and it will extract facts at a speed no human team could match.

Much of the current conversation about AI agents in property management turns on the need for a coherent data structure underneath them, so that agents working across maintenance, leasing and operations can reconcile their outputs instead of each acting on a partial view. I agree with that entirely. But a common schema solves only one part of the problem. It can organize the information. It cannot, by itself, tell us whether that information still describes the physical building.

That distinction is not hypothetical. Existing buildings are full of records that disagree with each other. One drawing puts a wall in one location and a later plan puts it somewhere else. The lease abstract carries one area and the measurement carries another. An equipment schedule lists a unit that was replaced years ago and never removed from the list. AI can read all of it. It still needs some way to know which version is true.

The physical world is the final authority

In my line of work we spend a great deal of time resolving exactly these discrepancies, and the answer is usually old fashioned. Go back to the building. Measure it, look at it, identify the equipment, confirm the space, record the condition.

The tools have changed enormously. LiDAR, mobile scanning, 360 degree imagery and computer vision have made verification faster, cheaper and far richer than it was even five years ago. The principle has not changed at all. For a physical asset, the physical world is still the only authority that settles an argument.

This is where I think the industry’s mental model of the stack is incomplete. The chain is usually described as software systems, then a common data model, then an AI agent. For existing buildings it needs one more layer underneath: the physical building, then verified ground truth, then the connected data structure, then AI. That extra step is the least visible part of the architecture and the part that lets everything above it earn trust. Without it, an outdated drawing, a stale equipment schedule and a current maintenance record all populate the same beautifully organized schema, and the result is wrong in a format that looks authoritative.

Provenance is about to matter a great deal

As AI takes a larger role in real estate decisions, I expect to hear far more about provenance. Where did this number come from? Who established it? Which standard was applied? When was it last verified? Has the building changed since then?

Those questions are familiar to anyone who works in building measurement, and they become considerably more important once machines are assembling answers from thousands of sources at once. A building record should not simply hold a value. It should hold enough context to explain why that value deserves to be believed.

My expert witness work has made this unusually vivid. Disputes involving floor area or measurement standards are almost never resolved by finding one more spreadsheet. They are resolved by understanding the source documents, the standard that applied, the physical conditions at the time and the method used to arrive at the number. AI can help organize that evidence and it can find inconsistencies a person would miss. But evidence and truth are not the same thing, and the distinction is going to matter well beyond litigation. It will matter in acquisitions, in leasing, in capital planning and in any decision where building data carries financial weight.

Let it say “I don’t know”

We have all become accustomed to software returning an answer. Building AI is going to need a different habit.

Sometimes the most useful answer is that the system does not know. Or that it found two conflicting sources. Or that nothing has been verified since the renovation. That is not a weakness in the product. It is the feature that makes the rest of it credible.

A system worth trusting should maintain confidence levels, surface conflicts rather than resolving them silently, and build a verification queue that someone actually works through. Over time every inspection, scan, service call and capital project improves the record. The result is never a perfect database, because buildings are too dynamic for that. What we can realistically build is a building record whose uncertainty is visible and managed rather than hidden.

The preparation happens in mechanical rooms

There is a great deal of talk about getting data ready for AI, and in most industries that means cleaning databases. In real estate it cannot mean only that, because we are dealing with physical assets.

Some of the most valuable AI preparation in this industry is going to happen in mechanical rooms, on rooftops, in tenant spaces and in parking garages, where the digital record finally meets the actual building. It is unglamorous work and it is not what anyone puts in a funding announcement.

Whoever solves that connection between physical truth and machine intelligence will have built something more valuable than another dataset. They will have built trust. Without it, talking to a building stays an impressive demonstration rather than a reliable way to run real estate.

The post AI In Property Management Has a Ground-Truth Problem appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Fatal Brooklyn Collapse Triggers Citywide Construction Site Audit
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
New York will inspect 100 construction sites after a Brooklyn building collapse killed eight people and injured 19 near an active development project.

The post Fatal Brooklyn Collapse Triggers Citywide Construction Site Audit appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
A three-story residential building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn collapsed Wednesday afternoon, killing at least eight people and injuring 19 others. The structure fell into an excavation pit created by construction at an adjacent property at 2625 Bedford Avenue, where a one-story building was being converted into a nine-unit apartment complex. Emergency crews continued extracting victims from the rubble hours after the 4:30 p.m. collapse, with one injured person remaining in critical condition as of Thursday afternoon. Among the dead were two children and two construction workers.

New York City officials announced a sweep of approximately 100 construction sites connected to the five entities involved in the adjacent development project. The Department of Buildings had issued a stop-work order for the Bedford Avenue site in March, but a follow-up inspection found the original building had already been demolished, resulting in a $10,000 fine. DOB Commissioner Ahmed Tigani said the agency is conducting a “whole-of-government investigation” while continuing to document evidence as debris is cleared. The collapsed building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue contained four apartment units and is owned by Isolag Realty Corp., which acquired the property in 2024.

The incident adds to mounting concerns about construction oversight in New York, where the city’s building boom has strained inspection resources. The planned audit of 100 sites represents one of the largest enforcement actions triggered by a single incident in recent years. Mayor Mamdani promised full accountability for any responsible parties, though the exact cause of the collapse remained under investigation as of Thursday.

City Plans 100-Building Inspection Sweep After Deadly Building Collapse

item.title: New York’s Right of First Refusal Law Adds Transaction Delays for Distressed Multifamily
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
New York's COPA law grants nonprofits first refusal rights on 2,100 multifamily buildings, adding transaction delays critics say discourage private investment.

The post New York’s Right of First Refusal Law Adds Transaction Delays for Distressed Multifamily appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act into law on Tuesday, requiring owners of certain multifamily buildings to notify the city before selling and grant nonprofits a right of first refusal. COPA takes effect in November 2027 and applies to roughly 2,100 buildings, including distressed properties with four or more units and smaller buildings subject to affordability restrictions. Eligible nonprofits have 20 days to submit a statement of interest and 70 days to make an initial offer. If an owner receives a competing bid from a private buyer, the nonprofit retains a right of first refusal.

City Council member Sandy Nurse, the bill’s lead sponsor, pushed the legislation through after former Mayor Eric Adams vetoed a broader version in December 2025. The original proposal would have covered 10,000 buildings. Nurse argued the city cannot build its way out of the housing crisis and must preserve existing stock. Manhattan Institute senior fellow John Ketcham countered that the law assumes nonprofit ownership is superior to private ownership without evidence that nonprofits manage maintenance or tenant relations better than private landlords.

A 2025 report from New York University’s Furman Center warned that opportunity-to-purchase laws impose timing delays and legal costs that can discourage investment, particularly in softer markets. Real Deal analyst Erik Engquist noted that nonprofits capable of acquiring distressed buildings already had access to them without the mandate, and COPA simply adds process layers rather than improving acquisition economics. The law follows the Mamdani administration’s rent freeze, which took effect last month, continuing a pattern of regulatory expansion in the city’s housing market.
